questions.questionText: Which term describes the people and assets located where a hazard may occur?
options: Exposure
Magnitude
Recurrence
Weathering
questions.correctAnswer: Exposure
questions.explanation: Exposure identifies populations, infrastructure and assets situated in places that could be affected by a hazard.

curriculum.objective: Analyse hazard risk as an interaction of physical processes, exposure, vulnerability, preparedness and recovery capacity.

questions.questionText: Why can earthquakes of similar magnitude produce very different death tolls?
options: Magnitude has no relationship to shaking
Vulnerability and preparedness differ between places
Every building responds in exactly the same way
Population distribution never affects hazard risk or mortality
questions.correctAnswer: Vulnerability and preparedness differ between places
questions.explanation: Building quality, density, response capacity and preparedness strongly influence impacts beyond physical magnitude.

curriculum.objective: Analyse hazard risk as an interaction of physical processes, exposure, vulnerability, preparedness and recovery capacity.

questions.questionText: Which measure most directly reduces coastal storm-surge mortality without preventing the surge itself?
options: Building more homes directly inside the storm-surge floodplain
Removing emergency communication systems
Reliable warnings and planned evacuation routes
Reducing the number of weather stations
questions.correctAnswer: Reliable warnings and planned evacuation routes
questions.explanation: Early warning and evacuation reduce exposure during the event even though they do not stop the physical surge.

curriculum.objective: Analyse hazard risk as an interaction of physical processes, exposure, vulnerability, preparedness and recovery capacity.

questions.questionText: A city rebuilds damaged infrastructure to higher standards and restores wetlands after a flood. Which resilience principle is illustrated?
options: Return every system exactly to its previous level of vulnerability
Transfer all risk without adaptation
Ignore future hazard probabilities
Build back better while increasing natural protection
questions.correctAnswer: Build back better while increasing natural protection
questions.explanation: Stronger reconstruction and restored wetlands reduce future vulnerability and improve adaptive capacity.

curriculum.objective: Analyse hazard risk as an interaction of physical processes, exposure, vulnerability, preparedness and recovery capacity.

questions.questionText: What is a transnational corporation?
options: A company operating in more than one country
A charity funded by one village
A government department without trade
A business serving customers only within one neighborhood
questions.correctAnswer: A company operating in more than one country
questions.explanation: A transnational corporation coordinates business activities across national borders.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate how trade, investment, migration and global production networks shape places and uneven development.

questions.questionText: How can foreign direct investment benefit a host region?
options: It always removes every local supplier
It can create jobs, capital and technology transfer
It prevents any infrastructure investment
It guarantees that every dollar of profit remains in the host economy
questions.correctAnswer: It can create jobs, capital and technology transfer
questions.explanation: FDI may add employment, finance, skills and technology, although benefits depend on linkages and governance.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate how trade, investment, migration and global production networks shape places and uneven development.

questions.questionText: Why may export-led economic growth fail to reduce inequality?
options: Exports automatically equalize every household income
Trade removes all differences in education
Gains may concentrate among owners, regions or skilled workers
Economic growth cannot change employment
questions.correctAnswer: Gains may concentrate among owners, regions or skilled workers
questions.explanation: Growth can be unevenly distributed when profits, opportunities and infrastructure favor particular groups or locations.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate how trade, investment, migration and global production networks shape places and uneven development.

questions.questionText: A clothing brand outsources production to several countries and changes suppliers quickly. What feature of global production does this show?
options: A fully local economy without external links
A fixed chain controlled only by consumers
The disappearance of comparative advantage
A flexible network coordinated across borders
questions.correctAnswer: A flexible network coordinated across borders
questions.explanation: Global firms coordinate dispersed suppliers and can relocate contracts in response to cost, risk and market conditions.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate how trade, investment, migration and global production networks shape places and uneven development.

questions.questionText: What is urbanisation?
options: An increasing share of people living in urban areas
The movement of every city resident to villages
A decrease in all settlement populations
The conversion of rainfall into runoff
questions.correctAnswer: An increasing share of people living in urban areas
questions.explanation: Urbanisation is the growth in the proportion of a population living in towns and cities.

curriculum.objective: Analyse urban growth, land use, inequality, mobility and regeneration as interconnected spatial systems.

questions.questionText: Why can improving a rail line increase land values near its stations?
options: Travel times necessarily become longer
Accessibility to jobs and services improves
Every business moves away from the route
Public transport eliminates all housing demand
questions.correctAnswer: Accessibility to jobs and services improves
questions.explanation: Better connectivity raises the attractiveness of nearby locations for households and businesses, increasing demand.

curriculum.objective: Analyse urban growth, land use, inequality, mobility and regeneration as interconnected spatial systems.

questions.questionText: Which policy best addresses spatial mismatch between low-income housing and employment centers?
options: Removing all bus routes from peripheral districts
Concentrating every job in inaccessible zones
Affordable transit connecting residents to job locations
Increasing fares without improving service
questions.correctAnswer: Affordable transit connecting residents to job locations
questions.explanation: Reliable affordable transport improves access when disadvantaged residents live far from available employment.

curriculum.objective: Analyse urban growth, land use, inequality, mobility and regeneration as interconnected spatial systems.

questions.questionText: A regeneration project raises environmental quality but displaces long-term low-income residents. What trade-off is most evident?
options: Higher rainfall versus lower relief
Primary industry versus tectonic stability
Map accuracy versus scale
Place improvement versus social equity
questions.correctAnswer: Place improvement versus social equity
questions.explanation: Physical and economic improvements can generate gentrification, creating conflict between investment gains and inclusive access.

curriculum.objective: Analyse urban growth, land use, inequality, mobility and regeneration as interconnected spatial systems.

questions.questionText: What is a carbon sink?
options: A store that absorbs more carbon than it releases
A source that releases only methane
A device that measures river discharge
A market where energy is sold
questions.correctAnswer: A store that absorbs more carbon than it releases
questions.explanation: Forests, soils and oceans can act as sinks when their carbon uptake exceeds their carbon release.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate environmental change and management strategies using systems, feedbacks, stakeholders and sustainability criteria.

questions.questionText: Why can deforestation create a positive feedback in climate change?
options: Trees permanently stop the greenhouse effect
Carbon release and reduced uptake can amplify warming
Bare soil always stores more carbon than forests
Warming automatically restores every forest
questions.correctAnswer: Carbon release and reduced uptake can amplify warming
questions.explanation: Forest loss releases stored carbon and removes future uptake, strengthening the processes that drive warming.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate environmental change and management strategies using systems, feedbacks, stakeholders and sustainability criteria.

questions.questionText: Which water-management approach most closely follows integrated river-basin management?
options: Manage each river section without sharing information
Ignore groundwater and land-use connections
Coordinate upstream and downstream users across the catchment
Give one user unlimited extraction rights
questions.correctAnswer: Coordinate upstream and downstream users across the catchment
questions.explanation: Integrated management treats the basin as a linked system and balances users, ecosystems and flows across locations.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate environmental change and management strategies using systems, feedbacks, stakeholders and sustainability criteria.

questions.questionText: A conservation policy protects biodiversity but removes local access to traditional resources. Which improvement best supports long-term legitimacy?
options: Exclude local knowledge from every decision
Use enforcement without consultation or compensation
Hide monitoring results from stakeholders
Co-design rules and benefits with affected communities
questions.correctAnswer: Co-design rules and benefits with affected communities
questions.explanation: Participation and fair benefit sharing can align conservation goals with livelihoods and improve compliance.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate environmental change and management strategies using systems, feedbacks, stakeholders and sustainability criteria.

questions.questionText: What does GIS allow a geographer to do?
options: Combine and analyse spatial data layers
Measure temperature without any sensor
Prove causation from one observation
Replace every field investigation
questions.correctAnswer: Combine and analyse spatial data layers
questions.explanation: A geographic information system stores, overlays and analyses data linked to geographic locations.

curriculum.objective: Use GIS, remote sensing, spatial statistics and research evaluation to investigate geographical patterns and decisions.

questions.questionText: Which remote-sensing data would best compare vegetation condition across a large region over time?
options: One interview from a city center
Repeated multispectral satellite imagery
A single handwritten weather note
An undated street photograph
questions.correctAnswer: Repeated multispectral satellite imagery
questions.explanation: Repeated satellite observations provide consistent wide-area coverage, while spectral bands support vegetation indices.

curriculum.objective: Use GIS, remote sensing, spatial statistics and research evaluation to investigate geographical patterns and decisions.

questions.questionText: A map shows high disease rates near polluted water sources. What additional evidence is most important before claiming causation?
options: Use brighter colors on the same map
Remove locations with low disease rates
Control for population, poverty and other confounders
Assume proximity proves the mechanism
questions.correctAnswer: Control for population, poverty and other confounders
questions.explanation: Spatial association alone may reflect confounding variables, so alternative explanations and exposure pathways require testing.

curriculum.objective: Use GIS, remote sensing, spatial statistics and research evaluation to investigate geographical patterns and decisions.

questions.questionText: A GIS suitability model weights slope 60% and road access 40%. Why should the weighting be sensitivity-tested?
options: Weights can never influence a model result
All criteria must always receive zero weight
Sensitivity testing removes spatial data
Different reasonable weights may change selected locations
questions.correctAnswer: Different reasonable weights may change selected locations
questions.explanation: Testing alternative plausible weights shows whether the decision is robust or depends heavily on subjective assumptions.

curriculum.objective: Use GIS, remote sensing, spatial statistics and research evaluation to investigate geographical patterns and decisions.
